cases.title: De novo PD-L1 nanobody design
cases.subtitle: Immune checkpoint · specified epitope
cases.result: Of 30 prioritized candidates, 26 showed binding activity in BLI, with a best affinity of 7.2 nM.

cases.subtitle: Membrane protein · complex target
cases.result: All 30 prioritized nanobodies were binding-positive in BLI, with a best apparent affinity of 23.2 nM.
cases.body: De novo design against the extracellular region of NK3R, with multi-stage computational screening to select the experimental candidates, extending binder discovery to complex GPCR membrane proteins.

cases.body: Candidate nanobodies are generated de novo and screened in multiple stages on structure and sequence properties; a small-scale experiment validated high-affinity binders.
cases.challenge: Candidate nanobodies are generated de novo and screened in multiple stages on structure and sequence properties; a small-scale experiment validated high-affinity binders.

structure.title: Assess structures and complexes from sequences
structure.lead: See how PD-L1 and the KN035 nanobody fit together

affinity.title: Prioritize mutations for improved binding
affinity.lead: Which mutations are worth testing first?
affinity.body: Start from the PD-L1 complex with the DBL1_03 binder (7XYQ). MoleculeOS scores 2,356 single-point substitutions on the binder chain and ranks them by predicted binding effect. Select a recommendation to see where it sits on the structure and which PD-L1 residue it faces, then decide what to test first.

stability.title: Improve expression, stability and developability
stability.body: Lock the CDRs, disulfide bonds and PD-L1 interface that hold binding, flag oxidation, deamidation and isomerization sites in the sequence, then screen only the framework: 75 positions, 1,425 substitutions scored by structure, sequence and evolution models. A shortlist with the trade-offs visible, each with its sequence-property check.

denovo.title:
Inspired by the known,
shaping the new
denovo.lead: Design new binders, no starting molecule needed
denovo.body: Start from the PD-L1 structure and the hotspots on its binding face. MoleculeOS generates new binder backbones and sequences (60–100 aa) from three independent seeds, predicts each complex and reports confidence and hotspot contacts. Three distinct computational designs to review before anything is ordered.

story.title:

case.title: PD-L1 × KN035
case.start: Starting from PD-L1 and KN035, turn your understanding of the molecule, step by step, into a basis for design, and give the next round of experiments a clearer direction

structure.title:
Starting from sequence,
see how molecules might meet
structure.lead: Predict the 3D conformation and likely binding mode, turning sequence information into a spatial model you can inspect
structure.body: Enter the PD-L1 and KN035 sequences, and MMFold generates five complex structure samples. Using the structures together with their predicted confidence, examine the binding interface to establish a starting point for further analysis and antibody optimization

mmetrics.title:
Into the interface,
finding clues for design
mmetrics.lead: Link functional regions, interactions and spatial positions, so structural details become checkable, designable evidence
mmetrics.body: MMetrics brings high-value data for understanding and analyzing a protein into one view. Descriptive data covers homologous proteins, enzyme active sites, antibody–antigen CDRs and epitopes, and interactions such as hydrogen bonds, π-π stacking, van der Waals contacts, salt bridges and π-cation; model-computed data adds mutation scores and more. On this complex it marks 19 epitope residues on PD-L1 and 18 paratope residues on KN035, with 44 interaction records, each tied to a position on the structure

affinity.title:
Every mutation,
with evidence behind it
affinity.lead: Look for mutations that may improve binding, combining mutation scoring with interface analysis to prioritize experimental validation
affinity.body: MoleculeOS predicts binding affinity for all 2,432 single-point substitutions on KN035. Among the interface candidates, V109L, Q116M and T105L rank highest. For each of the three, five complex structure samples were generated to examine the predicted interface more closely

stability.title:
Balancing binding and developability,
preparing candidates for the next stage
stability.lead: Variants that passed the affinity screen are assessed for structural, sequence and evolutionary fitness and scanned for risk motifs, so that binding potential is weighed against developability concerns
stability.body: With the sites involved in the two disulfide bonds held fixed, the selected mutations were assessed along several dimensions. Combining this round's scores with a risk screen, V109L is ranked as the priority candidate for validation; Q116M flags a potential methionine oxidation risk, and T105L shows weaker evolutionary fitness. Weighing binding potential against developability risk gives the next round of experiments a more complete basis

denovo.title:
Inspired by the known,
shaping the new
denovo.lead: Constrained by the target structure and a specified region, generate small binders unlike existing antibodies, opening new possibilities for molecular design
denovo.body: Taking the predicted epitope on PD-L1 as a reference, candidates 60–100 aa in length were generated. In the predicted complexes, all three candidates shown contact all 6 designated design hotspots, and cover 14–18 of the 19 reference epitope residues
denovo.verdict: All three pass the metric filters; you choose which to take to the bench.
denovo.note: For antibody, VHH or macrocyclic peptide design needs, feel free to contact us

faqs: What is an MCU, and how many does one run take?

MCU is the single unit all compute on MoleculeOS is metered in: in standard compute, 1 MCU is 1 effective compute minute, Heavy compute counts double, and queueing or waiting is not charged. A run costs what its effective compute time comes to; for example MMFold structure prediction is about 5 MCU, Binding Affinity Mutation Effect about 1.75 MCU and protein design about 0.33 MCU. See the pricing page for the estimates.
The free tier refreshes every month; when it runs out, top up as you go or upgrade your plan. An MCU costs ¥0.75 everywhere on the platform.

It does not read user data for any purpose unrelated to the service. When you start a computation, analysis or project action, the platform processes the data you enter or upload only to the extent needed for that function; security risk identification may also involve necessary processing under risk rules. Access is permission-controlled: only authorized personnel who need to know in order to deliver the service can reach it, and they are bound by confidentiality obligations.
What if different companies work on the same target?

The platform does not promise exclusivity on any target or research direction, and will not disclose one party's data to another because both study the same target. Because of public databases, model principles and similar inputs, different users may receive the same or similar outputs. Users should run their own patent searches, freedom-to-operate (FTO) analysis, experimental validation and compliance review; if a company needs target exclusivity or stricter project isolation, it should sign a separate written agreement.
How is data security and the confidentiality of uploaded data ensured?

Under the agreement, a user's unpublished information is protected as a trade secret. The platform applies reasonable measures no weaker than those it uses for its own comparable trade secrets, uses the information only for the services the agreement covers, and does not disclose it to third parties except as required by law or as the agreement provides. Internal staff and professional advisers who need to know are bound by the same confidentiality duties.
For personal information, the platform uses industry-standard safeguards, including encryption, trusted protection mechanisms and access control. The internet is never absolutely secure, so users should also keep their account, password and other credentials safe.
Who owns the results and any related patents?

Data that users enter or upload, and the result data the platform computes, analyzes or generates on their instructions, belongs to the lawful holder of that data. MoleculeMind holds, as the law provides, the intellectual property in the platform itself and its technical work, including algorithms, models, model weights, code, interface and documentation.
Does MoleculeOS train models on my data?

User business data is not used to train or tune protein design models.
To provide and keep improving the service, the platform uses operational behavior data for basic experience analytics, feature iteration, maintenance, risk control and account security; the agreement states that this use does not involve tuning protein design models. Mocha chat records are used to improve the product experience, and uploaded or imported files are used to complete tasks as instructed; neither is used to tune protein design models.

q55r.how: Arg could form a salt bridge with Asp89 and improve electrostatic complementarity
q55r.risk: The long Arg side chain may clash with neighbours

s31y.basis: Only a van der Waals contact with antigen C:Tyr81 (2.92 Å)
s31y.how: Tyr could π-stack with Tyr81 and add contact area
s31y.risk: L-CDR1 conformation may change; check the fold
s31y.exp: Re-measure KD by BLI / SPR; check thermal stability by DSF

n102d.basis: Van der Waals contacts with antigen C:Arg130 and C:Arg132 (2.39–2.71 Å)
n102d.how: Asp could form salt bridges with both Arg residues and add electrostatic complementarity
n102d.risk: More Asp in H-CDR3; watch isomerization (Asp104–Asp105 are already nearby)
n102d.exp: Re-measure KD by BLI / SPR and assess stability

s95a.basis: L-CDR3 Asn94–Ser95 is a deamidation-prone motif (NS)
s95a.how: Ser95→Ala breaks the NS motif and lowers deamidation risk; the site is not in direct antigen contact
s95a.risk: May slightly change CDR loop flexibility
s95a.exp: Forced degradation + LC-MS peptide mapping; re-measure affinity

g66a.basis: Framework Asn65–Gly66 is an NG motif with high deamidation propensity
g66a.how: Gly66→Ala breaks the NG motif; framework sites have little direct effect on binding
g66a.risk: Framework mutations can affect folding and stability
g66a.exp: DSF thermal stability + forced degradation; re-measure affinity

d104.basis: H-CDR3 Asp104–Asp105 carries an isomerization-prone motif (DD), but Asp104 also forms a salt bridge and H-bond with antigen Arg132 (3.63 Å / 2.64 Å)
d104.how: This is a key contact; mutating it directly is not advised
d104.risk: A mutation would lose a key salt bridge
d104.exp: Run accelerated stability first to confirm isomerization before deciding

tasks.title: Improve candidate binding
tasks.brief: G6 binds VEGF-A; make it stronger
tasks.situation: The G6 Fab already binds VEGF-A, but pushing affinity higher is costly trial and error. Structure limits which interface residues can move, and the combinations are too many to exhaust.
tasks.approach: Start from the 2FJG binding interface, generate a few informative mutation combinations on the contacting heavy- and light-chain residues, then rank and explain them.
tasks.outcome: An experiment-ready candidate list showing which interface residue changed in each candidate and why.
tasks.mediaTodo: 替换为亲和力优化的真实操作录屏

tasks.title: Improve expression, stability and developability
tasks.situation: G6 binds well enough, but expression, thermal stability or aggregation still falls short of development needs. If process and formulation fail, the earlier work is wasted.
tasks.approach: Lock the interface that contacts VEGF-A and search only the framework away from it, assessing each change for its effect on binding.
tasks.outcome: Modification proposals that leave the binding interface alone, each with a risk note.
tasks.mediaTodo: 替换为稳定性改造的真实操作录屏

tasks.title: Generate binders for a new target
tasks.brief: Design new binders, independent of G6
tasks.situation: To step outside existing antibodies and their epitopes, you start from the VEGF-A receptor-binding surface and look for new binders from scratch. Conventional routes rely on phage display or chance.

headline.text: Across 12 targets, with no more than 50 candidates tested per target under low-throughput conditions, target success exceeded 90%.

cases.subtitle: Immune checkpoint · specified epitope
cases.result: Of 30 prioritized candidates, 26 showed binding activity in BLI, with a best affinity of 7.2 nM.
cases.body: MMDesign generates nanobody candidates against a specified PD-L1 epitope and narrows large-scale designs to 30 experimental candidates by jointly weighing structural reliability, sequence properties and binding evaluation.

cases.category: De novo NK3R GPCR nanobody design
cases.subtitle: Membrane protein · complex target
cases.result: All 30 prioritized nanobodies were binding-positive in BLI, with a best apparent affinity of 23.2 nM.
cases.body: De novo design against the extracellular region of NK3R, with multi-stage computational screening to select the experimental candidates, extending binder discovery to complex GPCR membrane proteins.

cases.subtitle: Cytokine · small screen, high hit rate
cases.result: Testing only 14 candidates yielded 7 TNF binders, with a best apparent BLI affinity of 51 pM.
cases.body: Candidate nanobodies are generated de novo and screened in multiple stages on structure and sequence properties; a small-scale experiment validated high-affinity binders.

cases.subtitle: Histidine engineering · antibody optimization
cases.result: At pH 6.0, the optimized antibody dissociates about 62 times faster than at pH 7.4.
cases.body: Histidine site design combined with analysis of the protonation state of the binding interface tunes binding kinetics at different acidities, yielding experimentally validated pH-responsive candidates.

cases.category: Thermostability engineering of a sugar-substitute enzyme
cases.subtitle: Industrial enzyme · multi-objective optimization
cases.result: Half-life extended from 2.3 h to 200 h, with the melting temperature raised by 15°C.
cases.body: Sequence and structure analysis plus multi-objective mutation design around the enzyme's thermostability significantly improve its heat tolerance.

cases.subtitle: PISCO · Pichia pastoris
cases.result: Of 13 PISCO-optimized PRK coding sequences, 12 showed improved soluble expression in Pichia pastoris experiments.
cases.body: Protein 3D structure, amino-acid sequence and host codon preference are optimized together, designing host-adapted coding schemes without changing the protein sequence.

helpCenter.title: A method for every step of your exploration
helpCenter.lead: Browse the guides and learn from user cases to apply MoleculeOS analysis and design to your research
helpCenter.flowLabel: One research flow, seven entry points

cases.title: Set a goal, and let analysis and computation follow the task
cases.lead: You want to optimize an antibody, but first you need to prepare the structure, inspect the interface, assess mutations and then collate every step. With Mocha you describe the research goal and constraints directly; it breaks the task down, works out which models to call, and afterwards organizes candidates, scores and the rationale. You can follow the task as it runs, or open the raw results and keep checking.
body: In the project chat, provide the antigen, antibody heavy and light chain sequences, and state the goal and the regions that must stay unchanged. For example:
cases.prompt: Predict the structure from the given sequences and recommend 30 mutations that may improve antibody affinity, avoiding positions that already interact with the antigen.
after: After submitting, open **Task** to see status, duration and per-task details. When it finishes, read the key findings and recommended candidates first, then find reports, data tables and structure files in **Workspace**.

cases.title: From sequence to structure: a starting point for analysis
cases.lead: You have antibody and target sequences but no structure to analyze yet. With MMFold you can start a structure prediction from sequence, load the result into a MoleculeOS project, then inspect the molecular shape, locate residues and compare with other structures. If you already have a structure, upload it directly or load it by PDB ID.
steps: Format the input as FASTA as the model requires; for several chains, separate them with : on one line as the manual describes. After starting the MMFold job, open the task details to see the returned files: five CIF structures with their confidence JSON files. Download them and load them into the project to keep viewing and comparing.
Select one of the structures and click a residue in the sequence; the matching position is highlighted in the 3D view. From here you can analyze regions and sites on the same object.

cases.title: Around one molecule, find the research information worth noting
cases.lead: With the structure in hand, you need to confirm what each chain is, which regions deserve attention, and what homologous information is available. MMetrics organizes the loaded complex into a molecular description, homologous references, functional regions, interactions and mutation scores, so you go from the overview down to specific positions and build up your understanding of the subject.
steps: Once the antibody–antigen complex is loaded, MMetrics starts computing. First check the protein type, name, function, chain composition and the evidence behind each call in **Description**.

Then look at CDR, heavy/light chain and epitope annotations in **Annotations**. Click a region name to highlight it in the structure; click a single residue to locate it further. Build the overview first, then move on to homology search, interaction checks or mutation assessment as your question requires.

cases.title: Find homologous references to support the redesign
cases.lead: Before redesigning a sequence you want to know what related proteins can tell you: which positions are conserved, which vary, and which structural or functional information is worth reading further. SeqSim Search starts from a sequence or a chain in your project, then helps you find suitable references through filtering, multiple sequence alignment and source access.
steps: Open **SeqSim Search** from the bottom toolbar. With a structure loaded, choose **Search by chain**, pick the protein and chain, then click **Blast**; with only a sequence, use **Search by Sequence**.

When the job finishes, load the results into the project, review the match metrics and expand the hit sequences. If there are too many, narrow them with **Filter**; tick several related proteins and click **Align** to see how a region of interest varies across sequences. To check background information, go back to the source database through **Reference**.

cases.title: From structural differences to specific interactions: find sites worth checking
cases.lead: With references found, attention turns to specific positions: which local regions differ between structures? Which residues surround a candidate site, and what interactions do they take part in? In MoleculeOS you can align structures, inspect spatial neighbourhoods and non-covalent interactions, then save key positions and observations in the project.
steps: **Compare first, then focus.** With several structures, use Superimpose: set one as Fixed, the others as Moving, choose the chains to align and inspect local regions. After selecting residues of interest, use 5Å to filter neighbours by distance and amino-acid type; use Distance to check distances further.

**Then move from position to interaction.** Open Non-Covalent Bond to check hydrogen bonds, π–π stacking and π–cation interactions of the selected residues. To decide which positions to look at first, consult Hotspots, which ranks single sites by their number of interactions.

**Finally,** save key residues with Annotation: name them and write your observations, for example separate notes for “positions to keep” and “positions to evaluate further”, so they are easy to find again.

cases.title: Turn the evidence into candidates and compare every option
cases.lead: With structure, homologous references and key sites in place, the next step is to propose concrete substitutions and compare how they perform on different dimensions. MoleculeOS provides mutation scores along sequence, structure and evolution axes, and also supports binding-affinity mutation assessment. Around your research goal, get candidate recommendations and reasons from Mocha, or run sequence redesign on a region you specify.
steps: In **MMetrics → Mutation Scoring**, view or download `MutXseq.csv`, `MutXstruct.csv` and `MutXevo.csv` and check the chain, specific mutation and score on each dimension for every record. To assess binding affinity, specify the complex, the chain to scan and the partner chain as the model requires, create a scoring task through Mocha, and fetch the results from **Output Data**.

Submit the redesign scope and research constraints to Mocha and review the candidate positions, scores and reasons it gives. To redesign a specific region, start **Protein Redesign**, check the designed residues under **Input Data** in the task details, and download the generated FASTA sequences from **Output Data**.

cases.title: Keep results and observations in the project so the team can carry on
cases.lead: Once candidates are ready, the team still has to check positions, discuss the evidence and decide the next round of experiments. MoleculeOS organizes the related proteins, tools and tasks in the project; you can view or download result files, record key observations on sites, then invite members into the project to keep checking.
steps: Before a review, check the related computations in **Task** and fetch Mocha's reports, data tables and structure files from **Workspace**. Put the structures to discuss into the project and use **Annotation** to note the sites and explanations, so colleagues can jump straight to the right position.

A member with sharing rights opens **Share**, picks colleagues from the company and invites them with **Read / Edit**. Permissions can be adjusted later as work changes. Site annotations in the project can be viewed by members with access and kept up by members with edit rights.
